item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Overall, I must say that this story gave me an incredible amount of enjoyment.

I would like to say that if anyone reads this and hasn't yet read all the way through this masterpiece, I highly recommend it. While the main character (if he can be called that), Ruiz, isn't particularly interesting to me, I can happily say that it wasn't really much of an issue as there are so many wonderful characters here.

Something VERY impressive to me is how well the artists were done as characters. They felt real, like I could picture exactly what kind of person they'd be if you took away the anomalous stuff. They paint a realistic picture of what kind of person would be against foundation without making them all "Grah I'm an evil sociopath" or "I'm perfect and the foundation is evil."

spoilers!
I warned ya.

Pico is kinda "Grah evil sociopath" but he's written well enough to make up for that.

The way you worked Mister Redd and Wondertainment into this was pretty great as well, though I'm not sure I understood all of the stuff with Redd. Then again, I don't really have much of a grasp on Redd to begin with, probably since I never bothered to read up on the Scarlet King. (Tufto's Proposal scared me off with it's length. I'll get around it it someday.) Lack of understanding does not negate enjoyment all of the time, however, and it didn't do that here.

The bits at the end about suicide were confusing, and I wonder what exactly that was, but it was well written and enjoyable, like everything else.

Tan losing all his friends like that saddened me, and I wonder what exactly is to come of him now that he's Nobody. If this ever gets written, I wanna read it.

+24 (one for each part, and one for the hub)

item.title: Crazy Headcanon Time
item.content:encoded:
+ show block

The year: 2043
The location: a diner. Any diner. Maybe your local IHOP.
The cast: A few old men.
Premise: The old men, once enemies in a war fought behind closed doors and erased memories, sit down and discuss the, well, good old days, as Carol gets them their coffee. They talk about things that couldn't have been spoken of before. It doesn't matter now, the Veil is lifted, the secrets are out, it's done. What can anyone do, amnestitize them?
As they talk, they begin to realize something. Despite their now-moot feud, they have quite a bit in common. They've all lost friends, seen wonders and horrors, and did what had to be done. So, they talk. And they laugh, and cry, and shout, and eventually, they realize something. Everyone thinks they know what happened behind the Veil, behind the locked doors, the atrocities swept under the rug.
But they don't know the people, the heroes and war criminals and artists and toymakers and Nobody in particular. So the old men begin to write. They change names, intentionally muck up details, mix characters together, leave events out. After several months, including time finding contacts once long-forgotten and getting, if not the complete story, then at least the feeling, they're ready.
They publish under a single pen name, that they won't face any real consequences for their transgression. Their masterpiece? The Cool War: The Story of the Death of an Artist.
It becomes a bestseller. Try as it might, the Foundation can't stop it; without the Veil, they're not as good as they once were. The old men, once enemies, die happy, rich, and as friends.

Basically, this whole story is a semi-autobiographical work of fiction by former agents and anartists who sat down and talked about their old escapades.

-Makes sense, no?
